node.label: Liberal order framework
node.period_rationale: Extension entry (period null, like settler_colonialism and digital_history). Its state-formation roots (Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992) fall in period_3, and the prospectus appeared in December 2000 at the coverage boundary; its debate, reception and the property strand are after 2000.
node.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · coverage through 2000; mostly post-2000 extension

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1988 and 1992 are state-formation roots, not the framework's origin; the prospectus (2000) is the naming milestone; 2009 the debate volume; 2018 the latest selected property work. Neither endpoint bounds the programme.

node.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures, and Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
node.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Bannister, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).

representative_people.name: Ian McKay
representative_people.context: Proposes the framework: Canada as a project of liberal rule and liberal hegemony; in his 2009 reply holds that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated; continues it through a history of the Canadian left as a counter-project.
representative_people.works: “The Liberal Order Framework” (2000); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009); Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008)

representative_people.name: Bruce Curtis
representative_people.context: Historical sociologist of state formation through schooling, inspection and the census; Christie credits him with recasting the liberal order as governmentality. A root of the framework, not a follower of it.
representative_people.works: Building the Educational State (1988); True Government by Choice Men? (1992); The Politics of Population (2001); “After ‘Canada’” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012)

representative_people.name: Allan Greer
representative_people.context: Studies a feudal, largely self-sufficient habitant society in rural Quebec before 1840; coedits the state-formation collection Colonial Leviathan; later work on commons, enclosure and "property formation" carries the questions toward property and dispossession.
representative_people.works: Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Colonial Leviathan (1992), ed. with Ian Radforth; “Commons and Enclosure” (2012); Property and Dispossession (2018)

representative_people.name: Ian Radforth
representative_people.context: Coeditor of Colonial Leviathan; primary placement in English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history.
representative_people.works: Colonial Leviathan (1992), ed. with Allan Greer

representative_people.name: Fernande Roy
representative_people.context: Her study of Montreal's francophone business liberalism is named by Pâquet as one of the prospectus's two explicit sources, with Gramsci.
representative_people.works: Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988)

representative_people.name: Michel Ducharme
representative_people.context: Coedits the debate volume; his intellectual history of liberty in the two Canadas distinguishes republican and "modern" liberty before 1838.
representative_people.works: Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), ed. with Jean-François Constant; Le concept de liberté au Canada (2010; trans. 2014)

representative_people.name: Jean-François Constant
representative_people.context: Coeditor of the debate volume and coauthor of its introduction; editorial credit only.
representative_people.works: Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), ed. with Michel Ducharme

representative_people.name: E. A. Heaman
representative_people.context: Tests the framework through rights talk (read by Christie as doubting that liberalism was ever hegemonic); her history of taxation sets "the propertied versus the people" at the centre of Canadian political history.
representative_people.works: “Rights Talk and the Liberal Order Framework” (2009); Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017)

representative_people.name: Jeffrey L. McNairn
representative_people.context: Intellectual historian of public opinion in Upper Canada who answers the framework from intellectual history; his chapter is title-level only here.
representative_people.works: The Capacity to Judge (2000); “In Hope and Fear” (2009)

representative_people.name: Jerry Bannister
representative_people.context: Proposes a "loyalist order framework" for 1750–1840 (chapter title); how it relates to McKay's liberal order is not characterized here.
representative_people.works: “Canada as Counter-Revolution” (2009)

representative_people.name: R. W. Sandwell
representative_people.context: Finds "a-liberal" values persisting in families into the twentieth century and treats the family as a site where liberal order was contested.
representative_people.works: “The Limits of Liberalism” (2003); “Missing Canadians: Reclaiming the A-Liberal Past” (2009)

representative_people.name: Adele Perry
representative_people.context: Places women and racialized people in the making of liberal order; chapter read at title level only.
representative_people.works: “Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order in Northern North America” (2009)

representative_people.name: Jarvis Brownlie
representative_people.context: Names First Nations' relation to liberal order "a persistent antagonism"; title-level only. Published as Robin Brownlie (1994) and Robin Jarvis Brownlie (2009); the University of Manitoba profile gives Jarvis Brownlie (he).
representative_people.works: “A Persistent Antagonism: First Nations and the Liberal Order” (2009)

representative_people.name: Nancy Christie
representative_people.context: Accepts the framework's synthesizing value but faults its timing, its statism and its property-based individual, and asks for religion, voluntary associations and the family. Primary placement in religion, social reform and secularization.
representative_people.works: “Revisiting Canada’s Project of Liberal Rule” (2009)

representative_people.name: Bryan D. Palmer
representative_people.context: Marxist critique: as an elastic, trans-historical category liberal order lets historians avoid naming capitalism. Primary placement in Canadian working-class history.
representative_people.works: “Radical Reasoning” (2009)

representative_people.name: Jean-Marie Fecteau
representative_people.context: Round-table commentator who reconstructs McKay's separation of liberalism from capitalism and argues that liberty, equality and property are not a stable, unitary set.
representative_people.works: “Towards a Theory of Possible History?” (2009)

representative_people.name: Janet Ajzenstat
representative_people.context: Political scientist who, by her own account, reads Canadian constitutional "great texts" such as the Durham Report; objects that the framework rests on summaries of others' work rather than primary sources.
representative_people.works: “Historians in Search of a Framework” (2009)

representative_people.name: Bettina Bradbury
representative_people.context: Follows Montreal working-class families as wage labour and industrial capitalism remade family survival; read alongside the framework in PhD bibliographies, not an adherent. Primary placement in women's and gender history.
representative_people.works: Working Families (1993)

representative_people.name: John C. Weaver
representative_people.context: Comparative history of land appropriation and the emergence of property rights with the market economy; adjacent to the framework's property questions, not an adherent. Primary placement in settler colonialism.
representative_people.works: The Great Land Rush and the Making of the Modern World (2003)

representative_people.name: Mariana Valverde
representative_people.context: Marks the boundary with moral regulation, which the user decided is a different project; her moral-reform study is heavily co-cited with McKay's prospectus.
representative_people.works: The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991)

strands.title: State formation before the framework
strands.focus: Schooling, inspection, the census and the "colonial Leviathan" of the 1840s–60s studied as state formation. Curtis (1988) and Greer and Radforth (1992) predate the prospectus; Curtis's later books (2001, 2012) continue that work, and their relation to the framework is not checked here.
strands.works: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992); Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? (1992); Curtis, The Politics of Population (2001); Curtis, Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012)

strands.title: The prospectus: Canada as a project of liberal rule
strands.focus: McKay proposes mapping Canada as liberal hegemony to get past the social versus national-political impasse. Pâquet names Gramsci and Fernande Roy as its explicit sources.
strands.works: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (2000); Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988)

strands.title: Property, market society and capitalism
strands.focus: The editorial reason for separating this entry from moral regulation: the framework's individual is a property-holder, and its later work runs to land, enclosure and taxation. McKay distinguishes liberal order from capitalism; Palmer replies that the distinction lets historians avoid capitalism.
strands.works: McKay, “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009); Weaver, The Great Land Rush (2003); Greer, “Commons and Enclosure” (2012) and Property and Dispossession (2018); Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017)

strands.title: Liberty, public opinion and francophone liberalisms
strands.focus: Intellectual histories of liberty and deliberation that test whether "liberalism" was one thing: republican against modern liberty in the two Canadas, public opinion in Upper Canada, francophone business liberalism.
strands.works: Ducharme, Le concept de liberté au Canada (2010); McNairn, The Capacity to Judge (2000) and “In Hope and Fear” (2009); Roy (1988)

strands.title: Debating the Canadian liberal revolution
strands.focus: The 2009 volume tests the framework across rights, municipalities, conservation, the family, women and racialized people, First Nations and British Columbia; McKay replies with a long liberal revolution of the 1840s–1940s.
strands.works: Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009)

strands.title: Critiques
strands.focus: Loyalism rather than liberalism before 1840 (Bannister); a-liberal families (Sandwell); religion, gender and governmentality (Christie); capitalism avoided (Palmer); an unstable definition (Fecteau); thin primary evidence (Ajzenstat).
strands.works: Sandwell (2003, 2009); Bannister (2009); the Underhill Review round table (2009): Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet; Palmer (2009)

strands.title: The left as counter-project
strands.focus: McKay's history of Canadian socialist and left "formations" measures the left by how far it pushed liberal order "to its definitional limits" (as Palmer quotes him).
strands.works: McKay, Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008)

strands.title: Rural society, wage labour and the transition to capitalism
strands.focus: Social histories on either side of the transition, read alongside the framework in Canadian PhDs (Bradbury: 13 of 44 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000, lift 4.0; Greer: 5 of 16, lift 4.2). Greer finds habitant society in the Lower Richelieu, 1740–1840, organized around a feudal order with household self-sufficiency; Bradbury follows Montreal working-class families as wage labour and industrial capitalism remade family survival. Both predate the prospectus and are not checked as responses to it.
strands.works: Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993)

relation_to_periods: The main period is 1920–2000. Only the state-formation roots (1988–92) and the December 2000 prospectus fall inside it; the debate and the property strand are post-2000. Recommended as an extension entry with period null.

proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Pâquet names Gramsci as one of two explicit influences on the prospectus; Ajzenstat describes McKay as recommending "a Gramscian approach"; Palmer argues McKay's reading of Gramscian hegemony is too seamless. McKay's abstract uses "liberal hegemony" and "commonsense". PhD context: 9 of the 91 PhDs citing McKay 2000 also cite a Gramsci work. Influence on the prospectus only, not on every work in the roster.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Marxist labour historians charge the framework with avoiding capitalism
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Palmer: as a "seemingly trans-historical analytic framework" liberal order "sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism’s changing historical structures"; historians should name "capitalism as systematic exploitation". One critic's position; it does not speak for all labour historians. Source endpoint is a proposed entry.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Liberal order and capitalism: analytically separate, historically entangled
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Fecteau quotes McKay that liberalism and capitalism must be kept "analytically separate" (2000, 629) yet after the 1840s "could not be easily separated" (2009, 385), and quotes McKay in 1994 on a "liberal capitalist order … based on possessive individualism". A teaching comparison between historical-materialist categories and the framework, not a descent.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Property, land, taxation and market society
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Weaver relates property rights to the growth of democracy and the market economy; Heaman places "the propertied versus the people" at the centre of Canadian political history; Greer studies property formation. These carry the framework's questions into economic and social history. The atlas has no history-of-capitalism entry; see lof_rel_05.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Draws social and political history into a renewed political history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Parnaby: McKay argued that liberalism as a "project of rule" could draw social and political history into one problematique, and interest in that question has reinvigorated histories of political ideas, institutions, census taking, border making and tax collecting. A contribution, not a claim that it founded political history in Canada.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Governmentality as a reading of the liberal order
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Christie cites Curtis's point that what McKay describes is "governmentality", which she finds more precise; Curtis's Ruling by Schooling Quebec is subtitled "Conquest to Liberal Governmentality". The contribution runs through Curtis; whether McKay drew on Foucault directly is unchecked. PhD context: 7 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs cite Foucault's governmentality lectures.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Liberal rule and moral regulation: neighbouring, distinct projects
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". Pâquet links the framework to studies of "liberal social regulation", and Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender organization. PhD context: 27 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs also cite Valverde (lift 3.6). Comparison only; both endpoints proposed or new.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Offers a way past the social versus national-political impasse
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: McKay's abstract frames the prospectus as a way past "the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse in Canadian history writing"; Ajzenstat sets it against Granatstein's attempt to revive national history. An intervention in the debate's terms, not a party to every exchange in it. Target is proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Family and gender historians question a property-holding individual
proposed_relationships.map_label: Families, women and the liberal individual
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Sandwell: a-liberal values persisted in families, "hot zones" where liberal order was imposed, contested or rejected. Christie: McKay's "definition of individualism based on property ownership" excludes women. Perry's chapter title places women and racialized people in its making. Both endpoints are proposed entries.

Greer studies property formation and the dispossession of Indigenous peoples; Weaver the appropriation of land and the emergence of property rights in settler societies; Brownlie's chapter title calls First Nations' relation to the liberal order "a persistent antagonism". Comparison only: no checked source joins the two frameworks.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Francophone histories of liberalism and liberty
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Pâquet names Fernande Roy's history of francophone business liberalism as an explicit source of the prospectus; Ducharme's history of liberty in the two Canadas and Fecteau's critique carry the debate in Quebec scholarship. PhD context: Roy (1988) is cited by 16 PhDs, 8 at francophone universities. Target is proposed.

Curtis presents Ruling by Schooling Quebec as "A Historical Sociology" and Pâquet ties the framework to studies of state formation. Comparison only: no checked source links the Canadian work to the comparative historical sociology the atlas entry describes. Corrigan and Sayer's Great Arch is co-cited (6 of 10 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000) but unread.
